title: Landscape

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Wan-go H. C. Weng, 1955
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A tall hanging scroll landscape painted in black ink on paper, with layered brushwork in varied tones of gray and black. The scene is built up in soft and dark strokes across the vertical format.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, artist, date, medium, period (Qing dynasty), classification, public-domain flag, credit line and image URLs read from the record. The record has no tags or scene description, so the text stays at the level of ink landscape, tone and brushwork.

context: A hanging scroll titled Landscape, dated 1693, by Wang Hui, a leading painter of the early Qing dynasty who lived from 1632 to 1717 according to the Met. It is painted in ink on paper. Wang Hui is often grouped with other masters who studied and reworked the landscape styles of earlier centuries.

descriptions.k: This tall picture is a landscape made only with black ink. Some parts are very dark and some are soft gray. Can you find the darkest spot and the lightest spot? Pretend to walk into the picture.
descriptions.g12: Wang Hui painted this landscape in China more than 300 years ago. He used only black ink on paper. The ink makes dark, medium, and light grays. The scroll is tall, so your eyes can climb upward. Where would you start to look first?
descriptions.g35: Wang Hui was a famous painter in the Qing dynasty, and he dated this tall landscape 1693. He used ink on paper, with strokes that are dark in some places and pale in others. The shape of a hanging scroll lets your eyes travel from bottom to top. How do the many tones of ink create depth in the picture?
descriptions.g68: Wang Hui (1632 to 1717) studied the landscape styles of earlier masters and combined them into his own. This hanging scroll, dated 1693, uses only ink on paper, which means all depth, texture, and mood come from tone and brushwork. A tall format invites the eye to climb through the scene. How can a painter suggest space and surface using just shades of one ink?
descriptions.g910: Dated 1693, this scroll shows how an early Qing master built a landscape from controlled layers of ink. Wang Hui worked in a tradition of studying earlier painters, so brush marks and composition may echo older styles while serving his own vision. Consider how line, tonal gradation, and the vertical format create structure and depth, and how the viewer's eye is guided without color.
descriptions.g1112: Wang Hui's 1693 landscape exemplifies a Qing practice of absorbing earlier styles into a personal synthesis, so that viewing involves recognizing both quotation and invention. In monochrome ink, depth, atmosphere, and surface are produced entirely through brush handling and tonal modulation. The record gives no description of specific scenery, so interpretation should proceed from what can be seen. How do tradition and individuality coexist in a single scroll?

teacherNote.context: Wang Hui (1632 to 1717 per the Met) was a leading early Qing landscape painter. The record gives no description of the scenery, so ask students to describe what they see before discussing style.
directions: Have students make a gray scale of five ink or pencil tones, then use them to draw a simple landscape.
Ask students to describe the scroll aloud from bottom to top as if guiding a traveler.
Discuss the difference between learning from a master and copying.
